source.title: Scaling Laws for Multilingual Neural Machine Translation
source.authors: Patrick Fernandes; B. Ghorbani; Xavier García; Markus Freitag; O. Firat

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to supervised multilingual machine translation, a different training regime from language-model pretraining, and reports its own scaling and prediction results.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own held-out translation cross-entropy scaling results, predictions for trilingual models, and translation-quality metrics. It cites other scaling-law work in the background, but those cited results are not cataloged here. It does not test compute-optimal parameter-versus-token allocation, architectural-shape effects, or downstream task performance of pretrained language models.
record.test_reason: The study trains over 200 supervised multilingual encoder-decoder NMT models (20M–1B non-embedding parameters, near convergence, data-rich). It fits power laws in model size to their test cross-entropy, so its own results bear on whether the power-law form (V5) holds in a training regime other than LM pretraining. It does not measure LM pretraining loss, data or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, shape effects, or LM downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors add that language similarity has little effect on capacity sharing. Translating into English (XX→En) shows more positive synergy than En→XX. The fitted effective-parameter fraction can predict the full task trade-off frontier for any weighting and scale, including for ChrF and BLEURT.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines supervised multilingual encoder-decoder translation models, test cross-entropy, and translation-quality metrics rather than autoregressive language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Language-mixture weights change the multiplicative factor β; the authors report that the scaling exponent and irreducible loss remain within two standard deviations across weights. Translation direction changes effective capacity sharing, while related versus unrelated target-language combinations show no significant interaction difference. In-domain versus out-of-domain capacity splitting is mostly unchanged.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective parameter fraction per language pair differs by direction. For 5%-weighted tasks it exceeds 3× in En→XX and 6× in XX→En. Language similarity (De/Fr vs De/Zh) shows no significant difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multilingual MT, per-task effective capacity is scale-independent and depends on translation direction, not language similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing mixture weights changes only the coefficient β. The exponent α and irreducible loss stay within two standard deviations across weights (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multitask training, data-mixture weights shift the multiplicative factor of the scaling law but not its exponent.

record.problems: The study focuses on high-resource, data-rich translation and near-converged training, so it does not establish behavior in low-resource or compute-limited settings. Most experiments use two language pairs. For low-weight tasks, a convergence correction estimates performance at 2.5M steps for two models per scenario rather than training those models to that point. Some fit statistics and curves are presented only in figures; uncertainty in coefficient estimates is assessed by perturbing empirical data points, and the XX→En appendix omits uncertainty estimates as unreliable.
record.rows_left_out: The figures contain separate curves for multiple language weightings, test domains, and language-pair combinations. To stay within the row limit, the record keeps the reported aggregate fit results, key joint-fit results, and the trilingual prediction results rather than enumerating every plotted weighting-specific curve in Figures 2–5, 9–17, and 20. The study's language-similarity comparison and the detailed capacity-splitting curves are not separate claim-version results; the explicitly reported capacity examples are included as r13-r14.

untested.parts: Only model-size scaling in supervised multilingual MT, over about 1.7 orders of magnitude (20M–1B). Data and compute scaling are not tested, nor are image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Not tested: no LM pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no fit on small runs is checked against runs orders of magnitude larger.
Not tested: no fixed-compute parameter/token split is examined.
Not tested: encoder and decoder are scaled proportionally, and shape is not varied at fixed N.
Not tested: no downstream LM tasks are evaluated.
Not tested for published LM laws or fitting choices.

missing.what: Individual out-of-domain (newstest19) per-weighting fits: R² 99.95 (|ΔL| 0.017) and 99.97 (|ΔL| 0.017)
Joint-law in-domain fits. En→{De,Zh}: R² 99.84/99.79. En→{De,Fr}: 99.73/99.81. {De,Zh}→En: 99.94/99.94.
Exponent α and L∞ invariant across mixture weights (within 2 SD), with near-parallel log-log lines

record.verdict_notes: Scaling covers only model size, over about 1.7 orders of magnitude, with 8 model sizes or fewer. Low-weight largest models use a learning-curve convergence correction (Appendix G). The Figure 9 caption says En→{De,Fr}, but the panels show German/Chinese, an apparent caption error. The study is not an original source, so a V5 verdict is allowed.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures translation-model test cross-entropy, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
It does not report an experiment fitting a law on small language-model runs and testing predictions on much larger language-model runs.
It does not vary a fixed training-compute budget to find an optimal parameter/token split.
Architecture details are not independently varied at fixed parameter count.
The study tests supervised multilingual machine translation, not the other listed modalities and regimes such as image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
ChrF and BLEURT are translation-generation quality metrics in this study, not downstream task performance of pretrained language models.

The study examines changes in language-mixture weights and uses a convergence correction, but does not test whether published language-model laws disagree because of fitting choices or whether their curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: En→{De, Fr} multilingual NMT models
rows.operation_detail: Measured ChrF and cross-entropy as model size and language weighting varied.
rows.measure: Relationship between ChrF translation quality and cross-entropy
rows.value: The authors report an almost-linear relationship and say the fitted law captures the ChrF trade-off frontier almost as well as the cross-entropy frontier.
rows.note: This is translation-generation quality under the studied MT regime, not a downstream evaluation of a pretrained language model.
rows.check: Links to V5 only indirectly. The row shows ChrF is nearly linear in cross-entropy and that the joint law fits the ChrF frontier. It is not itself a loss-vs-size power law. evidence_form should be figure plus text (Fig. 8).

relationships.condition: Data-rich, near-converged multilingual NMT (En→{De,Zh}, En→{De,Fr}, {De,Zh}→En), 20M–1B parameters, in-domain and newstest2019 test sets
relationships.reason: Per-weighting power laws fit test cross-entropy with R² of 99.92–99.98 (r1–r6). Joint laws fit out-of-domain test sets (R² ≈ 99.7, r7–r8). Two-pair laws predict trilingual losses (r9–r10). Quality metrics track loss nearly linearly (r11–r12).
relationships.display_finding: Per-weighting laws achieved reported R² values of 99.92–99.98, joint out-of-domain fits reached approximately 99.7, and two-pair laws predicted trilingual losses.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested high-resource, data-rich multilingual NMT settings, including in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation
reader_labels.reason: The reported per-language scaling fits and joint fits describe test cross-entropy across model sizes and language weightings; two-language-pair laws also predict trilingual results (r1-r10). Translation-quality analyses show similar scaling behavior for ChrF and BLEURT (r11-r12).
